  "text": "In March the lighthouse door was planed down by a man who charged her nothing. He left the shavings in a pale curl on the step. For several nights Maren pulled too hard, expecting resistance, and the door opened against her foot.

That was one thing changed.

There were others. A boat was sold. The shop began closing on Wednesdays. Erris grew tall enough that her heels touched the ground when she sat on the harbour wall.

Sometimes she forgot to ask the time.

Maren went up regardless.

One afternoon she took a cloth to her mother's stone. Rain had gathered in the cut of the name. She worked the cloth into each letter, then stood with it damp in her hand. She had brought nothing to say. The grass needed trimming at the edge, and she did that with the small scissors from her coat.

On her way home she bought six bulbs in a paper bag. The woman in the shop said she was late planting them.

"I know," Maren said.

She put them in the strip of earth below her kitchen window. Nothing came of them for weeks.

Then one morning, washing a cup, she saw a green point where there had been none.

That night the harbour was hidden by rain. She wound the clock and entered the date beneath the date before it. There was room on the page for another month.

At home she left her muddy shoes beside the back door.

Before bed she set a clean cup out for the morning."

  "text": "The first flower opened while Maren was away buying bread. Erris saw it before she did and waited on the back step, though she had been told not to miss her dinner.

“Only one,” she said.

Maren put the loaf on the table and came out.

It was yellow, bent slightly towards the glass. There was soil on the lower leaves. Erris reached to brush it off, then looked at Maren.

“Leave it,” Maren said. “The rain will do that.”

They stood a little longer. Then Maren cut the end from the loaf, wrapped it in paper, and sent her home.

By June four of the bulbs had flowered. The other two gave leaves and nothing more. Maren kept watering the whole strip.

One evening Erris came with her to the lighthouse. On the stairs she went ahead, running her fingers along the wall until they came away white.

At the top Maren showed her where the key was kept. Erris wound the clock slowly, stopping twice to ask whether that was enough. Maren listened, then nodded.

In the book, beneath the day's date, Erris wrote her name. The last letter slipped below the line.

“Will I cross it out?”

“No.”

Coming down, they found a moth resting inside the door. Maren held it open while Erris coaxed the moth onto her sleeve and carried it outside.

It stayed there all the way to the harbour wall. They sat together until it flew, and then a little longer, because the stone was still warm."

  "text": "Years later, when the lighthouse clock was taken out, Erris helped carry it down. It was heavier than she remembered anything being. On each landing she and the workman set it between them and waited for their hands to stop aching.

Maren had asked for the key.

“They might need it,” Erris said.

“Ask.”

The workman left it on the kitchen table. For a time Maren kept it beside the bread knife, where it caught crumbs in the hollow of its stem. Then she put it in a drawer.

The new light came on by itself. Maren watched it from the back step the first evening, with her coat over her shoulders. When it swept across the harbour, she went inside to finish washing up.

After her death, Erris found the key while looking for string. She was tying together the books that were to go to the harbour office. In one she found her own name, the last letter still hanging below the line.

She left the page open while she made tea.

Outside, the narrow strip beneath the window had become crowded. She had meant to lift the bulbs that autumn, but there had been the roof to mend, and then Maren's illness, and the ground had hardened before she thought of them again.

Now a yellow bud was showing among the leaves.

Erris took her tea onto the step. Tomorrow she would separate a few bulbs and carry them home in a paper bag. She would have to clear a place first.

She sat considering where."
